comments.author: anself
comments.text:
Most of these issues are vastly improved or mitigated by adding clear instructions in AGENTS.md.
I follow a specific process with agents, and it works reasonably well:
1) describe my intended feature or change and then say “please recapitulate my intention and write an implementation plan”
2) read the plan carefully and refine it, make any corrections
3) tell the agent to go, but I check in frequently as it’s going. I watch the stream of thought and make course corrections or pull it out of rabbit holes
4) carefully review the result. Checking that tests actually fail, removing unnecessary changes
5) add instructions in AGENTS.md if I’ve found a new behavior that needs redirection

> Inability to change the response style
In recent months, I’ve been noticing a new pattern in sentence structure more and more often. Here are some examples:
There’s a difference between "I read the text" and "I understood the meaning of the text".
We too often mistake "I’m used to this" for "I like this".
The path from "I’m afraid of making a mistake" to "I’m ready to try" can take years.

I could provide examples but the whole point is that you can tailor it to exactly how you want it. This has the added bonus of being a quick sanity check for model quality. comments.author: neuwirth
comments.text:
This is built on VerInf, work that I did as a MARS fellow. They ripped everything down to the choice of 400B Maverick from us with very little attribution. Cool, I guess...

comments.author: vessenes
comments.text:
I've been writing about the need for provable inference (and training) on and off for a number of years; this is welcome news and a good start, and a significant improvement on prior zk results.
The problems of inference proof for a closed model provider are more difficult than an open model provider -- you can get a probabilistic proof much more cheaply out of four independent inference providers running the same non-batched prompt than this 90-100x compute hit.
Anthropic and others also have a significant problem with these proofs in that they have a lot of incentive internally to have some portions of the pre-prompt secret; I haven't read this newest scheme closely enough to determine if they have a way to hide parts of the prompt with the proof. But if they don't, they are almost certainly not going to want to send these proofs out in the general case.
Last, I'll take this moment to soapbox and say for the researchers out there -- provable inference is nice. Provable training corpus information would be spectacular. It would be very, very, very nice to provide a set of model weights and a proof that they had only been trained on a dataset. To be clear, this is a really hard pro

comments.author: gopalv
comments.text:
> In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers?
> the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.
> The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's check
I know they mentioned $ETH in the technical report, but this is exactly the mechanic for a crypto currency Proof-of-Work which is expensive by design.
When they announced it, I was hoping for a 5% overhead validation that the model that served you is really Fable and not Opus.
The quantization bit caught me out, because we saw the boundary crossing from good-context-size to bad is so sharp it feels like longer context requests are sent to quantized models to make more room for more KV-Cache. This would expose those sorts of tricks people can play to have the same GPU do better on short context benchmarks and gracefully degrade on long context.
At work, we did a bit of digging[1] into exactly why BaseTen, Fireworks and Together serve Inkling weights

comments.author: nemo1618
comments.text:
For open-weight models, provable inference is trivial: just redo the computation! This is much faster, cheaper, and doesn't require any fancy cryptography, just deterministic inference (which, if you read carefully, the ZKP approach needs too). See
https://lukechampine.com/repligraphs
Of course, it's unlikely that we'll get open-weight models from OpenAI or Anthropic any time soon. That means we have to choose between a) fancy ZKPs, b) signed responses, or c) comparing results from multiple inference providers.
Whatever method ends up being used, it's clear to me that
some
form of provable inference is inevitable. People haven't caught on to its more significant applications, but they will. (This post touches upon one of them: model-driven audits.) Think about it:
we can prove that a particular mind authored a particular artifact.
That's never been possible before! You can't prove that Melville wrote Moby Dick, for example; but you
can
prove that Claude wrote a poem, or that Gemini approved a pull request, or that GPT got a particular score on some eval. This is a more powerful primitive than a cryptographic signature.

We prove an exact integer version of the published weights, and a proof asserts that each checked token is that model’s greedy choice. A reply from a floating-point implementation, or sampled decoding, could depart at some position...

stories.title_en: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander

comments.author: daniel_rh
comments.text:
Author here: in 2015, I was playing the classic Wing Commander in DOSBox and
suddenly realized the game state fit in the 64k data segment.
Over ten years my brother and I went through a set of experiments (stop
and go, turn, communicate) while probing the memory. We uncovered
where the variables were, how to inject calls into
the game functions, and how to sync the gamestate across the
network, so we can fly the story missions together.
My favorite finding is that the camera lives in entity slot 0x3D, which is
possibly a "3D" reference by the original developers.
You can play it at
https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox
in browser. If
you own Wing Commander, drag in the installer since no game files are
hosted. If you don't, the page will load the original DOS/3Dfx version
of Vega Strike, before I open sourced it. I upscaled and redid DOS Vega
Strike art using AI, but it now has multiplayer and a similar feel.
I'll be in the lobby for the next few hours if anyone wants to fly together.
Disclosure: I also used AI for the final step to help compile for the
browser and port our TCP networking stack to WebRTC with voice and solve
a few lingering bugs.
